title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Show me a developer's 10-year cumulative operating cash flow beside its 10-year net profit, and I will tell you whether it is compounding capital or merely rolling inventory.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Principle

web_blocks.html: A twelve-year forensic review (FY15–FY26, plus TTM Sep 2026) shows rapid P&L scale paired with working-capital drag and modest return ratios [8]. Consolidated revenue rose from ₹165 crore in FY15 to a ₹277–382 crore plateau across FY16–FY21 [8]. It then jumped 3.1x from ₹347 crore in FY21 to ₹1,090 crore in FY26 and ₹1,247 crore TTM (Sep 2026) [8][10]. Over FY21–FY26, operating profit tripled from ₹95 crore to ₹299 crore (OPM 27–31%) [8]. Net profit expanded 5.1x from ₹31 crore to ₹157 crore (₹180 crore TTM) [8][10]. Interest expense fell from 63% of operating profit in FY20 (₹66 crore on ₹105 crore EBITDA) to 24% in FY26 (₹73 crore on ₹299 crore EBITDA) [8].

On the balance sheet, total assets more than doubled from ₹1,176 crore in FY15 to ₹2,594 crore in FY26 (₹2,515 crore in Sep 2026) [8]. 'Other Assets' dominate at ₹2,290 crore as of Sep 2026, reflecting work-in-progress inventory, land, and receivables [8]. Borrowings peaked at ₹968 crore in FY20 against ₹638 crore net worth (~1.52x D/E) [8]. Debt then declined to ₹808 crore (FY24), ₹676 crore (FY25), ₹711 crore (FY26), and ₹654 crore in Sep 2026 [8]. Management reports ₹646 crore gross debt and 0.44x D/E, aided in Q2 FY27 by divesting its 36% stake in Ultra Tech Property Developers Pvt Ltd [14]. In FY25, a ₹225 crore preferential issue of 31.64 lakh shares lifted equity capital to ₹39 crore and reserves to ₹1,167 crore [8][12]. On January 14, 2026, the company also completed a 1:5 share split from ₹10 to ₹2 face value [44]. Promoter holding shifted from 74.20% to 68.56% by Sep 2026, with a negligible 0.02% pledge [8][43]. CRISIL reaffirmed its Crisil A-/Stable rating on August 4, 2026 [1][25]. However, committed receivables from sold units now cover 82% of balance construction cost, down from 100% earlier [32]. CRISIL also flags ₹1,465 crore of planned incremental debt to fund ₹4,865 crore of FY27 launch costs, alongside ₹123 crore FY27 and ₹232 crore FY28 debt maturities [32]. Its downgrade trigger sits at debt-to-adjusted-CFO above 3.0x on a sustained basis [32].

Cash Conversion & Footnote Balance-Sheet Forensics: Despite strong headline PAT growth, 12-year cumulative Operating Cash Flow (FY15–FY26) is only ~₹461 crore [8]. That equals ~53% of ~₹870 crore cumulative net profit over the same period [8]. FY21 (₹201 crore CFO), FY23 (₹135 crore), and FY24 (₹220 crore) delivered strong cash inflows upon project handovers [8]. However, FY25 CFO dropped to ₹8 crore (21% CFO/EBITDA) and FY26 CFO was ₹69 crore (47% CFO/EBITDA vs. ₹157 crore PAT) as new launches absorbed cash [8]. Return ratios also remain modest: 3-year average ROE is 11.9% (TTM ROE 11.5%, ROCE 14.3%) [8]. Working Capital Days stood at 591 days in FY26, with Debtor Days elevated at 142 days [8]. Off-balance-sheet footnote obligations are equally critical. Consolidated contingent liabilities surged nearly 60x in four years—from ₹7.64 crore (FY22) and ₹9.99 crore (FY23) to ₹157.13 crore (FY24), ₹276.57 crore (FY25), and ₹456.89 crore in FY26 (~31% of net worth) [35]. On February 17, 2026, management approved a ₹125 crore related-party corporate guarantee for associate Ajmera Bora Associates (67%-owned via Laudable Infrastructure LLP) for an ARKA Fincap facility [36]. On September 10, 2026, the Board also cleared an enabling resolution for up to ₹500 crore in private-placement NCDs [38]. Finally, 60%-owned Bahrain subsidiary Ajmera Mayfair Global W.L.L. carries a qualified FY26 audit opinion citing Bahrain Companies Law general-assembly non-compliance [37]. Investors must police management's FY27 guidance that D/E could rise back toward 1.0x to fund the Wadala Boutique Office and 8 planned launches [10].

web_blocks.mechanism: Held massive Mumbai land banks and Slum Rehabilitation (SRA) / airport-slum entitlements on paper, but funded slow-moving approvals and working capital with high-cost corporate debt while cash conversion lagged accounting profits.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Debt swelled past ₹7,000+ Cr as project approvals and TDR monetization stalled; interest coverage collapsed, leading to loan defaults and NCLT insolvency admission in 2019 with near-total equity wipeout.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Paper GDV in Mumbai (such as Kanjurmarg) cannot service debt on its own. Ajmera's decision to raise ₹225 Cr equity and cut D/E to 0.44x avoids HDIL's leverage trap—provided management honors its 1.0x gearing ceiling in FY27.

web_blocks.title: Forensic Checklist: Ind AS 115, Contingent Liabilities & Gearing
paragraphs: 1. Ind AS 115 & Receivables Coverage: Committed sales pending recognition stood at ₹1,550–1,850 Cr in FY26–H1 FY27, but CRISIL's August 4, 2026 rationale shows committed receivables cover 82% of balance construction costs (down from 100%), making fresh bookings and collections essential [10][14].

2. Off-Balance-Sheet Guarantees & NCD Capacity: Consolidated contingent liabilities rose to ₹456.89 Cr in FY26 (~31% of net worth), including a ₹125 Cr associate corporate guarantee (Feb 2026), while the Board also secured a ₹500 Cr NCD enabling resolution (Sep 2026) and CRISIL models ₹1,465 Cr of planned incremental project debt [8][10].

3. Gearing & Subsidiary Audit Watch: Re-leveraging from 0.44x toward 1.0x in FY27 is manageable if pre-sales hit ₹2,200 Cr and debt-to-adjusted-CFO stays below CRISIL's 3.0x trigger, while the FY26 qualified audit opinion at the 60% Bahrain subsidiary warrants monitoring until overseas repatriation completes [10][14].

book_paragraphs: Now you and I turn to the financial forensics—the part of the audit that separates genuine compounding from accounting optical illusions. If you look solely at Ajmera's income statement from FY21 to FY26, the recovery looks like a textbook turnaround: sales up more than threefold to ₹1,090 crore, operating margins holding a respectable 27% to 31%, and net profit multiplying 5.1 times from ₹31 crore to ₹157 crore (and ₹180 crore on a trailing twelve-month basis through September 2026). Even interest expense, which used to consume over 60% of operating profit in FY20, fell to 24% of operating profit in FY26.

Yet when you flip the page to the cash-flow statement, a more sobering reality emerges. Across the entire twelve-year span from FY15 through FY26, Ajmera generated roughly ₹461 crore in cumulative operating cash flow against ₹870 crore in cumulative net profit—barely 53% cumulative cash conversion. In FY25, net profit was ₹126 crore while operating cash flow was just ₹8 crore; in FY26, net profit was ₹157 crore while operating cash flow was ₹69 crore. Why? Because in growth-mode real estate, every rupee collected from an older tower gets immediately poured into the excavation, steel, and Mivan formwork of the next tower.

That working-capital hunger also explains why Ajmera's return on equity has averaged just 11.9% over the past three years (11.5% trailing) and return on capital employed sits at 14.3%, despite near-zero land cost in Wadala. Over ₹2,290 crore of 'Other Assets'—largely inventory and receivables—sits on the balance sheet, with working capital cycling at nearly 591 days and debtor days at 142 days. Footnote forensics add an important layer of caution: consolidated contingent liabilities climbed nearly sixtyfold from ₹7.64 crore in FY22 to ₹456.89 crore in FY26—roughly 31% of net worth—including a ₹125 crore related-party corporate guarantee approved in February 2026 for associate firm Ajmera Bora Associates. Meanwhile, CRISIL's August 2026 rationale notes that committed receivables from sold inventory now cover 82% of balance construction costs (down from 100% a year earlier) and models ₹1,465 crore of planned incremental debt over the project tenure to fund the ₹4,865 crore FY27 launch slate, backed by a ₹500 crore NCD enabling resolution approved in September 2026. Add a qualified FY26 audit opinion at the 60%-owned Bahrain subsidiary (Ajmera Mayfair Global W.L.L.), and you can see why headline 0.44x debt-to-equity understates true balance-sheet commitments.

You should also keep an eye on the subtle shift in shareholding and capital structure. Promoter ownership stepped down from 74.20% to 68.23% during the FY25 preferential issue (and ticked up slightly to 68.56% by September 2026 with a negligible 0.02% pledge), the company executed a 1:5 stock split to ₹2 face value in January 2026, and institutional DII and FII participation remains tiny at under 2% combined. That means Ajmera is still very much a promoter-anchored mid-cap where balance-sheet discipline—specifically keeping net debt inside the 1.0x ceiling and debt-to-adjusted-CFO below CRISIL's 3.0x downgrade threshold—matters far more than short-term earnings beats.

book_callouts.title: Why 11.9% ROE Demands Discipline
book_callouts.text: A business earning 11.5%–14.3% returns on capital cannot afford prolonged idle land like Kanjurmarg or slow-moving luxury inventory in Versova. Asset turns—launching, selling, and collecting quickly—are the only lever that lifts ROE toward 18%+.

book_callouts.title: The 53% Cash-Conversion Reality Check
book_callouts.text: Across twelve years (FY15–FY26), Ajmera converted just 53% of its cumulative accounting profit into operating cash flow. Never value a developer on peak P&L earnings without checking working-capital absorption.

book_subsections.title: The Base-Rate Lesson from Mumbai's Past
paragraphs: Mumbai real estate history is littered with developers who mistook land-bank appraisals for liquidity. HDIL once boasted tens of millions of square feet of Mumbai and SRA rights, yet collapsed into insolvency in 2019 when stalled approvals met high-cost debt.

Ajmera is in a far healthier position today—with 0.44x on-balance-sheet debt-to-equity, a Crisil A-/Stable rating, and 82% construction-cost coverage from committed receivables—but surging contingent liabilities (₹456.89 crore in FY26), ₹1,465 crore of planned incremental project debt, and Kanjurmarg delays are precisely why you should watch consolidated leverage and off-balance-sheet guarantees like a hawk.
